title: Security
note: Treat every input as hostile and every permission as a liability. Injection and XSS happen when data is interpreted as code, so keep data and code separate with parameterized queries and output encoding. Store passwords with a slow, salted, one-way hash such as Argon2id, and give each component only the access it needs.

read.title: When data becomes code
text: Many classic attacks share one root: the program lets data cross into a place where it is treated as code. In SQL injection, a login form builds a query by pasting in the user's text, and an input like ' OR 1=1 -- rewrites the query's logic. Parameterized queries fix this at the source, because the database receives the query structure and the values separately and never reparses the values as SQL. Cross-site scripting is the same mistake in the browser: unencoded user text becomes a script tag. Encoding output for its context, plus a Content Security Policy, keeps it inert.

Password storage follows a different rule: never keep anything that can be turned back into the password. A hash is one-way, but fast hashes such as SHA-256 let an attacker test billions of guesses per second. OWASP recommends slow, memory-hard algorithms, Argon2id first, with a unique random salt per password so identical passwords produce different hashes and precomputed tables are useless.
Finally, assume something will fail. Least privilege limits what a compromised account can touch, and defense in depth means one broken control does not open everything.

q.q: Why do parameterized queries stop SQL injection?
o: Values are sent separately and never parsed as SQL

q.q: What makes SHA-256 a poor password hash, per the reading?
o: Its speed lets attackers test huge numbers of guesses
It can be decrypted with a key

q.q: What does a unique salt per password achieve?
o: It lets the server recover passwords
